# Multilevel models
::: {.callout-tip icon=false}

## Example

Imagine that you are a researcher interested in the musical self-concept of young adults. You want to examine whether there is a connection to weekly duration of practice on their instrument.

So you gather a sample. You manage to find 15 youth ensembles that contribute to your study. For simplicity, let's consider that there are 10 players in each ensemble.

:::

## The idea behind multilevel models
The sampling strategy described in the example is called <em>multistage sampling</em> [snijdersMultilevelAnalysisIntroduction2012, p. 7]. It is a cost-efficient way to sample, as you can imagine how much more work it would be to sample only one person from one ensemble.  
The resulting data is called <em>nested</em> or <em>nested</em>, which means that the units of interest (e.g., musicians) are grouped in units on a higher level (e.g., ensembles) [snijdersMultilevelAnalysisIntroduction2012, p. 7].  
Statistically, you may not ignore this fact because it leads to dependent observations on the lower level.
One possibility to account for this fact is the use of <em>multilevel models</em>.
